extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, contest organizers, math-circle leaders, and readers interested in history/culture of mathematics education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed practices for designing and running pre-college mathematical competitions and enrichment activities, drawn from Russian/Soviet traditions and Konstantinov's work. Useful for organizers, problem-setters, and educators planning contests, camps, or math-wrangle style events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor long-answer 'Olympiad' style problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions ... emphasized long-answer 'Olympiad' style problems, rather than the short answer problems more typical of American competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because copying/printing was limited, problems were written or given orally, leading to an emphasis on problems that require developed written solutions. Long-answer problems encourage deeper reasoning, fuller exposition, and richer solution methods; they are appropriate when the competition infrastructure supports longer timed/extended work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include both novice and sophisticated solvers
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems ... are selected so as to include both novice problem solvers and those with sophisticated background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing a contest or set of problems, deliberately balance items so the event is accessible to newcomers while still challenging advanced students. This supports wider participation (e.g., 'Tournament of the Towns') and cultivates talent at multiple levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oral rounds and oral problem administration when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Many competitions included rounds that were conducted completely orally ... judges wrote the problem statements on a chalk board. They then explained the problems orally, taking questions from the audience to make sure the problem statements were clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral administration can ensure clarity, adapt problems to audience needs via Q&A, and is useful when printing/duplication is impractical. Organizers should train judges to explain problems and manage clarifying questions without giving away solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure problems are clearly describable and presentable
rubrics_metrics.description: We decided not to use [the cube wire-frame problem] ... How would the contestants express their solution? They would have to describe the motion of the cube as it passes through the plane. Some motions... are difficult to describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid problems whose solutions require cumbersome or ambiguous verbal/graphic description. Favor problems whose intended solution steps and arguments can be communicated and assessed clearly in the contest format to avoid confusion or unfair grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select problems that allow layered depth and introduction to advanced ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A third problem was about the 'Devil's Staircase' ... It was decided that there is enough here to offer students who have not had an introduction to analysis. The analytic implications of the results could be appreciated as they learned more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose problems that have entry-level aspects for novices but deeper avenues for advanced exploration, enabling use in teaching as well as competition and allowing students to grow into more sophisticated reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer problems with potential real-world or cross-disciplinary applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An Olympiad problem ... about packing polyhedra ... A student solved this problem, and brought it home to his father, an engineer. The father then used it to design tilings for ceilings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems that connect to applied contexts can motivate students and demonstrate mathematical relevance. While not required, application-minded problems can enhance outreach and show practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-day problem-solving followed by presentations (math wrangle format)
rubrics_metrics.description: They then explained the problems orally ... Finally the students were given three days to solve the problems and present them in math wrangle format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing extended time and requiring formal presentation develops deeper problem solving and communication skills. Organizers should provide clear presentation formats (math wrangle rules), judging rubrics for presentations, and sufficient time for preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize competitions by locality (Tournament of the Towns model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament of the Towns ... Competition is by ‘town’ (city). In the tradition of Russian/Soviet competitions, problems all require solutions written out...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A locality-based structure fosters local community involvement, team identity, and scalable participation. When adopting this model, require written solutions to preserve rigor and comparability across towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate classification of problems: suitability discussion among organizers
rubrics_metrics.description: We talked for two days about math problems. About ways to classify them. About which were suited for competition and which were not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem-setting should include explicit classification and discussion sessions among setters to decide suitability given the competition goals, audience, and format. Criteria for classification include describability, depth, accessibility, novelty, and potential for presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rounds or elements that emphasize oral presentation and defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The tradition of math battle or math wrangle ... evolved partly from this circumstance. ... Later, at the camp itself, I witnessed the process ... the contestants gathered ... judges wrote ... asked questions ... students present ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate events where students explain and defend solutions orally to build exposition skills, encourage dialogic problem solving, and allow assessment of understanding beyond written answers. Provide moderators/judges trained to evaluate both correctness and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate community structures (summer camps, math circles, seminars) as core to talent development
rubrics_metrics.description: Summer camps for students, after-school math circles and study groups, all became part of a tradition of enjoying mathematics ... Konstantinov’s work was central to numerous other initiatives ... Lomonosov Tournament ... Independent University of Moscow ... continued working in Moscow High School 179 ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained community activities—camps, circles, seminars—are central to nurturing problem-solving culture. Organizers should integrate competitions with ongoing enrichment programs, mentorship, and communal storytelling to sustain interest and share practices.
